newsitem.title: JAPAN: Taiwan pork crisis seen pushing up Japan prices.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan pork crisis seen pushing up Japan prices.

text.p: Wholesale pork prices in Japan have climbed sharply after Taiwan halted pork exports last week due to highly contagious foot and mouth disease, and Japan said on Monday it is monitoring the price rises.

"Pork is now traded on a commercial basis. But we'd like to ask for local traders' cooperation if price rises become excessive and local consumers suffer," Vice Agriculture Minister Masayuki Takahashi told reporters.
Taiwan's Council of Agriculture halted pork exports on Thursday after confirming the outbreak in the island's large hog population, dealing a blow to a major export industry.
On Friday, Japan's Agriculture Ministry indefinitely banned all pork imports from Taiwan, its largest supplier.
Due to the loss of Taiwan supplies, the wholesale price of pork in Tokyo rose by more than 10 percent to 463 yen per kg last Friday, traders said.
Prices are likely to rise further this week, they said.
Japan imported 653,176 tonnes of pork in 1996, the Finance Ministry said. Of that, 266,225 tonnes, 40.7 percent, came from Taiwan.
Japan's increased dependence on imported pork due to falling domestic output since the 1980s was also behind the rising wholesale prices of pork, industry officials said.
Imports have grown from 13 percent of total consumption in the 1982/83 fiscal year to 37 percent in 1995/96.
In 1982, Japan suspended pork imports from Denmark for a year and a half due to foot and mouth disease.
"The impact on domestic prices should be much bigger this time, given the increased imports," a pork trader at a major trade house said.
Domestic pork breeders are unlikely to boost production for environmental reasons, industry officials said.

Nagasakiya Co Ltd, a major supermarket in Japan, said it suspended sales of Taiwanese pork since last Friday. "We're shifting to domestic and U.S. pork to make up for the loss of Taiwan supplies," a Nagasakiya spokesman said.

Nagasakiya currently depends on Taiwan for more than 50 percent of its pork. "Our top priority at the moment is to shift to alternative sources as soon as possible. But we have no immediate plan to raise retail prices," he said.
The spokesman refused to comment on how many tonnes of U.S. pork the company was seeking in the wholesale market.
Daiei Inc, another major supermarket in Japan, is feeling less of an impact. It depends on domestic breeders for about 75 percent of its chilled pork supplies.
